summary: Specifies an EAP mechanism for authentication and session key distribution using the GSM Subscriber Identity Module. It enhances GSM authentication so multiple authentication triplets can be combined for stronger keys. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Your mobile phone has a tiny card that proves who you are. This memo lets that card prove your identity to other networks, like Wi-Fi, as well.

questions: how to authenticate with a sim card
subtitle: How a phone's GSM SIM card can prove who you are to any network that speaks EAP, such as Wi-Fi.

tldr.problem: GSM authentication has no mutual authentication, and its 64-bit Kc key is too weak for data networks. Yet operators want SIM credentials to work for network access beyond the cellular radio.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-SIM runs inside EAP. The server gets 2 or 3 GSM triplets, the peer adds its own random NONCE_MT, and all the Kc keys are hashed together into a Master Key. Messages are protected with a MAC, and an optional fast re-authentication skips the GSM infrastructure.
tldr.outcome: EAP-SIM gives mutual authentication and keys of up to 128 bits of strength, but only as long as the Kc values stay secret. The IESG note says the IETF did not review its security claims, and EAP-AKA is recommended where 3G infrastructure exists.

today: RFC 4186 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFCs that obsolete or update it. Its own text points to RFC 4187 (EAP-AKA) as the more secure alternative when 3rd generation identity modules and networks are available.

sections.title: Why EAP-SIM Exists
sections.content:
RFC 4186 defines an EAP-SIM method for the Extensible Authentication Protocol (RFC 3748). It uses the GSM Subscriber Identity Module (SIM) to authenticate a user and to hand out session keys.

GSM authentication is a challenge-response scheme. The SIM runs the operator's A3/A8 algorithms on a 128-bit random number (RAND) and a secret key Ki, and produces a 32-bit response (SRES) and a 64-bit key Kc. GSM has no mutual authentication, and a 64-bit Kc is not strong enough for data networks.

EAP-SIM fixes this by using several RAND challenges to produce several Kc keys and combining them. The client also contributes its own random NONCE_MT, which acts as its challenge to the network. The spec also includes optional identity privacy and an optional fast re-authentication.

The IESG note says EAP-SIM was developed by 3GPP and is published as information. The EAP working group only checked that it is compatible with EAP. No other review was done, and the IETF did not review the security of the cryptographic algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIM card can answer a secret quiz, but the old quiz was easy to crack and only the phone had to prove itself. EAP-SIM asks several quiz questions at once and makes the network answer too.

sections.title: The Full Authentication Exchange
sections.content:
The authenticator first sends an EAP-Request/Identity. After the peer answers, the EAP server sends requests of EAP Type 18 (SIM). Each carries a Subtype and a list of attributes in Type, Length, Value form.

  • Start (Subtype 10): the server lists the EAP-SIM versions it supports in AT_VERSION_LIST. The peer replies with AT_SELECTED_VERSION and its random AT_NONCE_MT.
  • Challenge (Subtype 11): the server sends the RAND challenges in AT_RAND and a message authentication code in AT_MAC.

The server obtains n GSM triplets, where n = 2 or n = 3, usually from the Authentication Centre (AuC). Triplets MUST NOT be re-used, except in some error cases. The peer runs the GSM algorithm, recomputes the MAC and checks it. If the MAC does not match, the peer sends an EAP-Response/SIM/Client-Error and the exchange ends.

Because the peer's NONCE_MT feeds into the MAC, the peer can tell that the message is fresh and that the sender holds valid triplets for the subscriber. If all is well, the peer answers with its own AT_MAC covering its SRES values, and the server sends EAP-Success.
sections.plainLanguage: The network says which secret handshakes it knows, the phone picks one and throws in a random number of its own, and then both prove they know the secret. If anything looks wrong, the phone walks away.

sections.title: Identities and Privacy
sections.content:
GSM subscribers are identified by the IMSI, a string of at most 15 digits. In EAP the identity is written as a Network Access Identifier (NAI), such as username@realm. EAP-SIM uses three kinds of username:

  • Permanent: normally the digit 1 followed by the IMSI, for example 1295023820005424.
  • Pseudonym: a temporary name issued by the server, used on full authentication to hide the permanent identity from eavesdroppers.
  • Fast re-authentication: a one-time name that the peer MUST NOT re-use.

The server sends new pseudonyms and re-authentication identities inside the encrypted AT_ENCR_DATA attribute of the Challenge. The server can ask for an identity with AT_PERMANENT_ID_REQ, AT_FULLAUTH_ID_REQ or AT_ANY_ID_REQ. The RFC discourages relying on EAP-Response/Identity, because an EAP framework may alter it and that breaks key derivation. It RECOMMENDS the method-specific attributes instead.

An active attacker may send AT_PERMANENT_ID_REQ to learn the real identity. A conservative peer holding a pseudonym can refuse with a Client-Error, while a liberal peer always answers. Up to three Start rounds are allowed in one exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of shouting your real name in a crowded room, the network gives you a nickname to use next time. A trickster might ask for your real name, so a careful phone can say no.

sections.title: Fast Re-Authentication
sections.content:
Full authentication needs 2 or 3 fresh triplets from the Authentication Centre, so it is a poor fit for frequent use. Fast re-authentication is optional, uses no A3/A8 algorithms and needs fewer round trips. It reuses the K_aut and K_encr keys from the last full authentication and derives a fresh Master Session Key from the original Master Key.

The server starts it with EAP-Request/SIM/Re-authentication, carrying an encrypted AT_COUNTER, an encrypted server nonce AT_NONCE_S and a MAC. The counter is an unsigned 16-bit number set to one on full authentication. It must be greater on every later re-authentication, which limits replays and the number of re-authentications between full ones.

The peer checks the MAC and the counter, and answers with the same counter value and its own MAC. If the counter is not fresh, the peer includes AT_COUNTER_TOO_SMALL, and the server falls back to a full authentication with a new Start. The server can also fall back to full authentication if it does not recognise the re-authentication identity.
sections.plainLanguage: After showing your ID once, you get a quick-pass ticket. Showing the ticket is faster than the full check, and each ticket has a number so an old one cannot be used again.

sections.title: Key Generation
sections.content:
On full authentication the Master Key is a SHA-1 hash of the identity, the n Kc values, NONCE_MT, the version list and the selected version. Because version data is hashed in, an attacker who tampers with the version negotiation causes the peer and server to derive different keys, and the MAC check fails.

The Master Key seeds a pseudo-random function (from FIPS 186-2) that produces K_encr (128 bits), K_aut (128 bits), a 64-byte Master Session Key (MSK) and a 64-byte Extended Master Session Key (EMSK). K_aut protects AT_MAC and K_encr protects AT_ENCR_DATA. The first 32 bytes of the MSK can be used as the Pairwise Master Key for IEEE 802.11i.

On fast re-authentication the same K_aut and K_encr are kept. A new MSK and EMSK come from a seed built from the identity, the counter, NONCE_S and the Master Key.

Hashing the Kc values together means that learning one session key does not reveal the original GSM Kc values.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone and the network mix several small secrets and a random number into one big secret key, a bit like stirring colours into a paint that cannot be un-mixed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of EAP-SIM rests on the secrecy of the Kc keys. An attacker who knows the n (2 or 3) triplets of a subscriber can impersonate a valid network to the peer. With physical access to the SIM it is easy to obtain triplets, and malware on the peer or attacks between the EAP server and the HLR are other routes.

Some A3/A8 algorithms, such as COMP-128 version 1, have been compromised. If the same credentials are also used in GSM/GPRS, the effective key strength can drop close to GSM level. The ultimate strength of derived keys is never more than 128 bits, because Ki is 128 bits.

EAP-SIM does not provide channel bindings, so it authenticates only the EAP server. A malicious peer could flood the Authentication Centre with requests, so servers SHOULD limit that traffic. Where reuse of triplets is a concern, the RFC advises using EAP-AKA.

The security claims section lists mutual authentication, integrity protection, replay protection and key derivation as supported. It lists ciphersuite negotiation, fragmentation and channel binding as not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole system is only as safe as the secret inside the SIM. If a thief copies the secret, they can pretend to be the network, so guarding it is the most important job.
